title: Replace the pressure regulator when the finished system—not just the valve—supports it
description: Compare readings, leak location, repairability, connection length, unions, access, and thermal expansion before choosing replacement.
answer: Replacement is strongest when the body leaks, pressure cannot be controlled, parts are unavailable, or repeat service costs approach a correctly matched new installation.
urgency: Changing a regulator can alter closed-system pressure behavior. The expansion-control and water-heater side of the system must be considered.
diagramAlt: Pressure regulator decision split between serviceable cartridge and full valve replacement
identifiers: Match nominal pipe size and the exact end-to-end connection arrangement.
Check the documented adjustment range and flow capacity.
A direct replacement footprint can reduce repiping but does not remove code checks.

choices.label: The body or bell leaks
choices.detail: Full replacement becomes more likely than an adjustment.

choices.label: Pressure cannot be stabilized
choices.detail: Confirm readings and upstream supply before selecting the new valve.

choices.label: The cartridge or strainer is serviceable
choices.detail: Compare the documented repair kit and finished labor cost.

steps.title: Document the old footprint
steps.body: Measure size, union arrangement, direction, clearance, and access.

steps.title: Verify the diagnosis
steps.body: Separate supply restriction, thermal expansion, and valve control failure.

steps.title: Price the complete change
steps.body: Include isolation, fittings, valve, pressure setup, leak check, and related expansion work.

stopConditions: Severe corrosion around the service entry
notThisDevice: A low shower flow alone does not prove regulator failure.
Replacing the regulator does not repair a restricted service line.
A potable backflow assembly has separate testing obligations.
